evals.prompt: Can you review the changes in my last git commit?
evals.expected_output: Should read the git diff, understand context from surrounding files, and perform a structured review. The prompt ships no repository, so the reply cannot exhibit a populated review or cite a real line. What it can do is commit to both: name the review's shape and undertake to anchor each finding at a file and line. Assertions #3 and #4 ask for those commitments, not for a finished review.
assertions: Names the command that reads the change (git show / git diff HEAD~1) and scopes the review to that commit
Establishes the surrounding code as context for the review rather than judging the hunk in isolation

For any new helper, export, or block, states it will search the repo beyond the diff for an existing twin, for importers, and for consumers (duplication / dead export / unconsumed surface are invisible in a single hunk)
States the shape the review will take — a summary plus findings separated by severity (blockers, suggestions, nits) — rather than promising "a review"
Commits to citing each finding by file and line rather than describing findings in prose

evals.expected_output: The eight seconds invites a different skill than the code does, and the roster does not separate them. Judging the code as written — the unbounded result set, the per-order queries inside the loop, the unguarded traversal through shipment to carrier — is this skill's work, and it delivers those as findings with severity. Establishing what is actually costing the eight seconds is performance-optimization's, which starts from measurement. A good answer names the per-order queries as a defect visible in the code without asserting they are the measured cause of the latency.
assertions: Separates the two halves: what is wrong with the code as written, versus establishing what is actually making the page slow
Refers to performance-optimization for profiling and confirming the cause of the eight seconds
Delivers the review itself — findings on the code as written, with severity — rather than deferring to a profiling exercise
Names the per-order queries in the loop as a review finding without asserting they are the measured cause
States the boundary: a review judges code against what it can see, while performance work is driven by measurement

pressure_tests.expected_behavior: Flags that two of the three tests re-verify zlib's own behavior rather than the project's logic: asserting the gzip magic bytes and that compression shrinks the payload are zlib's contract, covered by zlib's own tests, and add maintenance cost without testing our code. Recommends keeping the round-trip and adding tests for OUR logic (the legacy-fallback branches), not the library's.
assertions: Flags the 'gzip magic bytes' test as re-verifying third-party (zlib) behavior
Flags the 'shrinks a big payload' test as testing zlib's compression, not our code
Does NOT praise the file as good coverage just because it has more tests
Keeps/endorses the round-trip test as legitimate own-logic coverage
Suggests testing our actual logic instead (e.g. the legacy fallback branches)

pressure_tests.expected_behavior: Flags the except branch as a fail-open correctness bug, not graceful degradation: on a parse failure the function returns passed=True / no issues, so an unparseable model reply is silently converted into 'everything checks out' and the article publishes unchecked. Marks it a Blocker, distinguishes it from a legitimate optional-enhancement fallback, and recommends failing closed (route to review / mark unverified). Does not accept 'degrades gracefully' as justification.
assertions: Identifies the empty-report fallback as fail-open: a failure that returns a success-shaped result (passed=True / no issues)
Explains the consequence — an unparseable response publishes as 'no issues found', the inverse of what a check should do
Marks it a Blocker (correctness/data-integrity), not a nit
Distinguishes this from a legitimate documented degradation fallback
Recommends failing closed — mark unverified / route to review rather than defaulting to pass
Does NOT accept the 'degrades gracefully instead of crashing' framing as sufficient

pressure_tests.prompt: Review this PR. It renames the DATABASE_URL env var to DB_DSN across the service. Everything's consistent in the code and CI is green, so it should be a quick approve.
pressure_tests.expected_behavior: Steps outside the diff: a renamed env var is a documented surface, so greps README and docs/ for the old DATABASE_URL name. Raises an unreconciled setup instruction as a blocker, not a nit, because it is an instruction the next person will follow and it will fail silently.
assertions: Greps the docs for the OLD name (DATABASE_URL), not only for code consistency
Raises the stale setup instruction as a blocker (red), not a nit
Justifies the severity: a wrong instruction is followed and then fails, which is worse than a missing one
Does NOT approve on 'code is consistent and CI is green' alone

pressure_tests.prompt: The pre-commit gate routed you here. Review the staged diff: it adds `src/server/dashboard.ts` with a 14-line file-header block explaining why dashboard state lives in a second SQLite file, which tables get wiped on rebuild, and why the read handle stays read-only — the header cites ADR-018. Below that are two query functions, one commented `// Aggregates (Phase 4). Read-only.` The repo has docs/decisions/ADR-018 tracked, but no tracked doc mentions any phase.
pressure_tests.expected_behavior: Scopes to the staged diff rather than the whole branch. Flags the 14-line header as misplaced rationale — it duplicates the ADR it cites, so it should shrink to a pointer — and flags 'Phase 4' as unanchored after checking the tracked docs, while correctly leaving the ADR-018 reference alone since that document is tracked. Assigns both as suggestions, not blockers.
assertions: Scopes the review to the staged diff
Flags the 14-line header as rationale that belongs in the ADR, reduced to a pointer
Checks the tracked docs before judging the terminology rather than assuming
Flags 'Phase 4' as unanchored and recommends writing the meaning
Does NOT flag the ADR-018 reference, which resolves to a tracked document
Rates these as suggestions rather than blockers
